![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/293593a043a7713d87a2f8ad8a2eaecee26b34288e4662bb4b2fce834e703e56.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{3},$ the vertical line $x=-1$ and the horizontal lines $y=0$ and $y=1$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=-1,$ as shown above. Which of the following integrals gives the volume of the resulting solid?
question.worked_solution:
Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of $y:$ 

$$
y={x}^{3}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt[3]{y}
$$

 

Also, notice that the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=1$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/600ef6d7265add5c669a29394e45facae040292ce19caad9dcae390979b604b9.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=-1,$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=\sqrt[3]{y}.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\sqrt[3]{y})-(-1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt[3]{y}+1)^{2}\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2/3}+2{y}^{1/3}+1)\,\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$
